No, I think you have covered– you and your colleagues have covered certainly the breadth of issues related to the Solid Waste Management Plan and many, many other sanitation issues. I would say that I just look forward to working with you over the course of the next many, many years that we have these chairs together and

make New York City a cleaner, healthier place for the future.

Thank you so much, and I apologize that 2.5 hours wasn't enough for testimony. I thank you everyone— oh, there's no one else here. I thank you all for your time. We will take a five-minute break and move on to our next panel. Thank you so much. [break]
[gavel] We are back. Can we have our next panel up? We were bringing up the Independent Budgeting Office.

Hi, good morning. I'm the Committee Counsel. I'll be swearing you in. Brian Cain, Assistant Director for Housing, Infrastructure and Environment, Ryan Dougherty, Lead Budget and Policy Analyst, and Elliot Jackson. Jackson— excuse me, Ontkush, I'm sorry— Assistant Data Manager, could you please raise your right hands? Thank you. Do you affirm to tell the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth in your testimony before the council members, and to respond honestly to council member questions?
I do.
Yes, I do. Thank you. You may begin when ready.

Good afternoon, Chair Sanchez. I am Ryan Dougherty, Lead Budget and Policy Analyst at the New York City Independent Budget Office. I'm joined today by Brian Cain, Assistant Director of Housing, Environment and Infrastructure, and Elliot Jackson-Ontkush, Assistant Data Manager. As you know, IBO is an independent, non-mayoral city agency that conducts fiscal and policy research. I appreciate the opportunity to discuss the city's curbside organics collection program today. Last Friday, IBO published a report titled Curbside Composting: Current Trends in New York City's Organics collection. My testimony will highlight key takeaways from this research as it relates to today's discussion on DSNY's Draft Solid Waste Management Plan, also known as the SWMP. As already discussed today, organic waste includes food scraps, yard waste, and other compostable materials. Organics represent roughly 36 percent of the city's residential waste stream. Yet in 2025, organics collections amounted to just 2.4 percent of residential waste collected. IBO's analysis found

that the city's mandatory composting program launched in October 2024 produced early progress, but the most meaningful gains were driven by fine-based enforcement. In April 2025, when fine-based enforcement began, weekly organics collection tonnage nearly tripled over the four-week. That sharp response suggests that fine-based enforcement is an effective tool to increase compliance. When enforcement was effectively paused later that month, momentum stalled for the rest of the year. From May through December 2025, the final months of the Adams administration, weekly organics tonnage declined by 43 percent. Interestingly, collections did not immediately revert down to pre-enforcement levels. This suggests that many residents continued composting once the habit was established. Overall, organics collections increased from 1.4 percent of residential waste in 2024 to 2.4 percent in 2025, a 68 percent increase. However, the gradual downward trajectory after the pause demonstrates that enforcement was effective at encouraging compliance, and without it, progress plateaued and then declined. Under the Mamdani administration, some fines were issued from January through March 2026. But it's been

roughly three percent of the levels seen at this time last year. As IBO highlighted in our testimony on the Preliminary Budget, the organics processing budget is underfunded. It decreases after fiscal year 2026 from $24 million to a baseline of $19 million, despite DSNY expecting program growth over time. Further, there has not been a major mayoral announcement to resume full enforcement and encourage compliance under the new administration. Organic waste collection has historically been more expensive per ton than trash or recycling collections, largely driven by the high cost of staffing trucks relative to the tonnage collected on a route. Trucks collecting organics compared with recycling or trash have similar staffing and fuel costs but collect fewer tons along their routes. This undercuts collection efficiency. A past IBO report found that in 2019, the average cost of organic collection was $602 per ton. By comparison, the cost of trash collection was $86 per ton and $167 per ton for recycling. Diverting organic matter from trash streams can reduce costs by increasing the efficiency of organics truck collections while reducing the volume of trash to be collected. DSNY's 2026 Zero

Waste Report includes organic projections through 2036. The agency expects a linear increase of collections roughly following the rate of annual gains from 2023 through 2025. By 2036, this would increase the current diversion rate of 2.4 percent up to 11.5 percent for organics, or about one-third of residential organic waste. DSNY's model used information on New York City's recycling program and curbside organic programs in places like Cambridge, Massachusetts, and the state of Vermont to inform its 10-year projections. These other programs had little to no enforcement in their early years. This suggests DSNY's model similarly assumes little to no enforcement for New York City's curbside organics program. IBO's findings suggest that collections could exceed DSNY's projections if full enforcement is resumed to help build up initial sorting habits. This would help reach the economies of scale IBO estimates organics collections would need to reach cost parity with recycling. Similarly, while the draft SWMP mentions enforcement as a concept, it does not expressly indicate whether DSNY will resume full organics enforcement going forward. IBO's report also provided a description of San Francisco's system.

They have the longest running and most successful curbside organic system in the country. San Francisco does not use fine-based enforcement. Instead, they first launched into the— when first launched in 2009, San Francisco properties paid for their trash pickup, but not their recycling or organics. This made it cheaper for properties to divert recycling and organics out of trash bins. While different, San Francisco's system and New York City's fine-based enforcement both created a financial incentive to divert organics with measurable results. IBO's testimony here today is intended to provide further information to the city council and the public. IBO does not make policy recommendations and does not take a position on the appropriate level of enforcement. Ultimately, the goal is to build up a culture of sorting organics, recyclable materials, and waste properly. In line with DSNY's projections to increase organics diversion rates, the evidence from last year strongly suggests that fine-based enforcement is an effective way to encourage compliance. The trajectory of the city's organics diversion rate will be heavily shaped by the decisions made in the months ahead around outreach,

education, and enforcement. We hope this analysis is useful to the committee. IBO is happy to answer any questions. Thank you.

Be great to have my mic on. Thank you so much. So, I understand that the recent report on curbside composting states that IBO will update earlier analysis on this issue. Your report states that the 2025 organics diversion rate was a mere 2.4 percent despite organics potentially making up up to 36 percent of the waste stream. Very sad. I'm looking at you, city. Very sad. How does that play into the overall cost of residential curbside organics programs?

This is like it used to– like you mentioned, this is something that IBO plans to update as we get more data from the mandatory program. So, it did just start last year. So we're waiting for more before we can compare to when the program was voluntary. However, as mentioned today, when we reach economies of scale, we should see cost savings.

Great. And when we do get that, if when you do start writing the report, if you can keep in the back of your mind what changes

we could make to make curbside composting more economical. Would really love to see that once we have, you know,–
[interposing] Absolutely, yeah.
a report. Can you describe what some of the most prominent costs, whether financial or otherwise, emotional, that are attributable to the practice of landfilling organic waste?

Yes, so currently in the city it costs approximately the same for an organics truck to collect. It's the same salary or same salary position. So whether it's an organics truck or a trash truck, it's the same staffing on the truck. So if the truck ends up not being full by the end of the route, then you're spending a lot more money on staffing for little waste collected. And that's currently– since the city is not seeing the participation rate that it was– you know, it's hoping for, that's currently attributing to a lot of the cost.

And the report mentions a pay-as-you-know [sic] collection system

providing financial incentives to residents for reducing their refuse volume by recycling organic waste. When y'all reviewed this type of program, what did y'all identify as some of the obstacles to its implementation, and how can New York City, if at all, prepare itself for some of these potential issues?

Right. So thank you for that question. Just to reiterate, IBO does not make policy recommendations as to which system is better. However, when we were looking at San Francisco, there's a key difference in that DSNY collects residential waste. In San Francisco, it's a private company that collects all of their commercial and residential waste. So their incentive is to make money and also reduce costs. So, they had initially had this program where it was save-as-you-throw, but the main finding in the report was that once they reduced the incentive, they also saw declines in their diversion rate. So, incentives were seen to increase diversion rates for organic waste.

Human psychology. Speaking of San Francisco, in your review of that program, were you able to identify the effectiveness, if at all, of any of their educational materials

being left at residences that helped increase diversion rates? How does this compare to the effectiveness of our education and outreach programs? And have you seen any other educational programs either in San Francisco or elsewhere that have shown to improve effectiveness?

Thank you for that question. So we did focus on San Francisco. We did not look into any other educational programs. However, San Francisco also tied incentives to– with their educational programs. So it was a dual strategy as DSNY is also trying to achieve at the moment. They're both important. This is what the findings show.
Great. And now I will turn this over to y'all. Are there any questions that you thought I would ask you that I did not ask you?
I think that the hearing before this was very informative, and I think a lot of my questions that I had were answered. Do you have anything you want to add? No, that was great. Thank you.
Well, thank you. I appreciate it.
Thank you very much.

And you— this– you guys can— what's a proper way to say this? I don't want to— this panel is dismissed. Get out of here. Sashay away. I'm sorry, my dears. Great. Alrighty [sic]. I now open the hearing for public testimony. I remind members of the public that this is a government proceeding and that decorum shall be observed at all times. As such, members of the public shall remain silent at all times. You're allowed to laugh. The witness table is reserved for people who wish to testify. No video recording or photography is allowed from the witness table. Further, members of the public may not present audio or video recordings or sing as testimony, but may submit transcripts of such recordings or your songwriting to the Sergeant-at-Arms for inclusion in the hearing record. If you wish to speak at today's hearing, please fill out an appearance card with the Sergeant-at-Arms and wait to be recognized. When recognized, you will have two minutes to speak on the legislation being heard today or today's hearing topics: Finalizing the

city's 2026 to 2036 Solid Waste Management Plan. If you have a written statement or additional testimony— if you don't finish and you wish to submit it for the record, please provide a copy of that testimony to the Sergeant-at-Arms. You may also email written testimony to testimony@council.nyc.gov. Again, that is testimony@council.nyc.gov within 72 hours of this during. Audio and video recordings will not be accepted. And now I'd like to bring up the first panel. Can I have Dennis Schock? Can I have Rhonda Keyser and Matthew Civello? I hope I said that correctly. Is it Civello or Civello? Civello. Thanks. Thank you. Great.

Good morning. Just– Good morning, Chair Justin Suarez– Sanchez, I'm sorry. I like to– I like to thank— take the opportunity to speak today. My name is Dennis Schock. I stand before you proudly representing Uniform Sanitation Association Local 831, the men and women who work tirelessly to keep the city clean, safe, and moving, especially during the most challenging conditions. I'd like to bring up some issues about equipment. One is the skid steer. Skid steer would like— I would like to address the skid steers. Are a multi— a force

multiplier in snow operations. One skid steer can perform the work of up to 16 sanitation workers over a 12-hour shift. These machines are essential in clearing crosswalks, bus stops, pedestrian pathways, public safety– public safety where it's most at risk. However, we currently do not have enough of the trailers that transport these units quickly to areas in need of most. Additional, we need to expand the training and more of these members to be qualified and operate this critical equipment. We strongly urge to invest in additional skid steers, transport trailers, operating training, and also allow for members to respond faster, to work efficiently and better to protect the public. Second, I want to raise the issue of serious concerns about quality of equipment and materials currently being used. Currently being used, our members work very— our work work— our members work on traction chains, plow blades, and replacement parts made up of inferior steel that is prone to failure. This leads— this leads to frequent breakdowns during the active operations, forcing equipment out of service at its worst possible times. We have seen firsthand higher-grade materials used in the past last longer

and perform better under extreme conditions. Local 831 returns— would like to return the higher quality materials, standards, investing in durability and reduced downtime, improve reliability, and ensure that members can stay on the streets longer doing their jobs. Sorry for going over.
You're all good. I–
[interposing] This is all something new for me.
You are all good. I will make sure we have the rest of the testimony and it will be in the written record. Thank you so much. Thanks, Dennis. I really appreciate it.
You have a great day now, and thank you for your time.
You too.

Good morning, Chair Sanchez and council staff. I'm Rhonda Keyser, Program and Policy Director for Cafeteria Culture, which you know. Thank you for this opportunity to comment on the DSNY's draft SWMP. We're deeply grateful for this city's commitment to expanding organics diversion and to funding community composting and compost education. We urge the DSNY, though, to prioritize

funding and expansion of local composting rather than relying heavily on co-digestion. Now, at Cafeteria Culture, our New York City public school students are shifting the trash culture across the city in schools one at a time. They're reducing school food waste at the source and processing cafeteria food scraps locally. To reduce school food waste at the source, we're piloting our Mindful Choice Meals initiative at New York City Public Schools across all 32 districts. In our pilot schools, our initiative has reduced overall cafeteria food waste by up to 50 percent, while increasing student cafeteria food consumption by as much as 45 percent, by simply allowing students to choose what they want to eat within the USDA guidelines. Now, to process cafeteria food scraps locally, in just one partner school, our newly hired compost coordinator has walked over 1,200 pounds of cafeteria food scraps to Compost Power's site at Polo Grounds, who— Compost Power also operates the Patterson Houses site that you mentioned earlier. Our students' participation in composting their own food scraps turns their daily cafeteria routines into climate action and community engagement by transforming a potential waste burden into a local

resource. We urge the DSNY to rethink their commitment in the SWMP to long-term expansion of co-digestion, which it sounds like they have today, and biosolids infrastructure through 2036. Co-digestion, as we know, plays an important role in managing our wastewater, but local composting of our food scraps reduces truck traffic, builds public participation, produces compost that is actually used in the city, and creates opportunities for local jobs and local worker stewardship, especially in schools and NYCHA communities. And if New York City wants to— wants organics diversion to succeed long-term, community compost has to be a core investment, not a supplemental program. Thanks again for your opportunity to testify.
Thank you so much for your testimony.

I'm Matthew Civello, Chair of the Manhattan Solid Waste Advisory Board, and I'm delivering testimony on behalf of all four SWABS. The SWABS support the diversion targets set in the draft 2026 Solid Waste Management Plan of 30.5 percent for DSNY-managed waste and 54.1 percent for commercial waste. On January 16th, we submitted

comments identifying six areas in the draft plan that we believe require remediation to increase the likelihood that these targets will be met. Those six areas are the need for increased and well-defined public engagement, the requirement that open datasets be clearly defined and consistently maintained, alignment with the CLCPA and Climate Action Council Scoping Plan and Local Laws 152, 86, and 87, a provision for a clear organizational and structural commitment within the Department of Sanitation to support recycling and sustainability, a recognition of emerging regulatory and legislative frameworks in New York State and beyond that call into question the feasibility of beneficial use of biosolids, and the need to move the plan's language towards clear stated program commitments rather than language that is merely exploratory. We will submit our full set of comments with some adjustments because there's a new draft, I guess, and our written testimony based— will be based on that for this hearing. There's not only a social and environmental benefit to diverting material from the residential waste stream, but also a fiscal one. While diversion will neither eliminate nor significantly reduce costs, since funding follows

material and diversion programs require investment in collection and processing, every dollar spent diverting material away from landfill or incineration has the potential to retain economic activity, create jobs, expand tax base, and increase public investment within the city. If we consider the fiscal spending on recycling and composting also as a form of fiscal stimulus with an associated non-trivial multiplier effect, we begin to see a more equitable distribution of both the burdens and benefits of shifting what is now nearly $600 million in export budget to recycling and composting within the five boroughs. I want to thank you for this opportunity to provide testimony.

Thank you so much. Thank you so much for your testimony. And with that, this panel is dismissed and I'd like to call up the next panel. Can I please have Marisa DeDominicis? I didn't want to mess it up. Justin Wood and Jenille Scott. Oh, and Eric Goldstein.
Lovely to meet you. Okay, where do I begin?
Thank you. Apologies. Okay, and with that, we can get started.

Good afternoon, Council Member, Chair Sanchez. And I was delighted to meet you and to hear the testimony from DSNY. It seems like we're off to a good start. I'm the E.D. and the Co-founder of Earth Matter. And I want to applaud all the efforts in the SWMP. The one area I'd like to emphasize is the parallel trend of commercial collection or mandating of waste diversion at the same time as rolling this program out. I think it's essential since they are contributing to 40 percent of the waste stream in New York, and I think that will be beneficial to the overarching plan. And now, my Earth Matter hat. We focus on education. We're on Governors Island. We diverted 700 tons that we processed from both Big Reuse, Lower East Side, and our very own Governors Island. We're a small compost facility, and we urge you in the SWMP to expand the language to say it's necessary to be able to invest in local, decentralized compost facility and the educational components that we, as well as the other communities community composting network organizations provide. We train over 90 groups. And when I say in 2014, we had a LaGuardia student make posters for her building, and the building

maintenance didn't put the compost bins back in the same area. I will say that that building maintenance, like Gale Brewer said, the certification program that Mr. Anderson had talked about is critical. Training, education, we need it. We need certification for the building owners and we need it for our young students and we need to expand what we can do. When Mr.-- the Sanitation talked about skid steer training, we do that at Earth Matter. Thank you very much and we look forward to working with you for a very long time.
Thank you so much for your testimony. There you go.

Hi, my name is Jenille Scott and I'm the Climate Director at ALIGN and a member of the Transform Don't Trash Coalition. Thank you so much to Chair Sanchez for the opportunity to present testimony today. We think that this solid waste plan, the draft solid waste plan, is really essential to shaping the future of waste in New York city for the next decade. I think that it— this plan needs to meet the urgency of the climate crisis as well as addressing longstanding environmental injustices and centering workers here in New York. We look forward to reviewing the updated plan, which we

learned is on the website as of Friday. But I think just to use this as an opportunity to uplift that the biggest concern we had was around the vagueness of the plan and how it was framed as a framework. We think it missed a lot of, like, timelines and benchmarks and things that were really essential. So we're hoping that those are things that are considered in the updated draft. And also wanted to use the opportunity to uplift the Transform, Don't Trash's People SWMP, which is a concrete list of 30 community-driven recommendations that our coalition worked to put together, and this includes suggestions around reducing truck traffic and getting to waste equity, full accountable implementation of the commercial waste zone program, which if if it's done before December 28th, we are okay with that, in 2027. Meeting the zero waste diversion goals, and making sure that's in line with the Climate Leadership and Community Protection Act mandates. Major expansion into compost and organics infrastructure, waste reduction and reuse policies, phasing out reliance on incineration, sustainable funding, environmental justice accountabilities, and equitable service provisions, especially for NYCHA residents. So, the

written testimony I'll provide will give a lot more details on all of those recommendations, but we think that the council has a really essential role to play in approving the final SWMP before it's sent to the state DEC. So we just really urge the council as we're reviewing this updated draft, that you're considering, like, the necessary specificity and accountability that is necessary in that plan, and to incorporate the 30 recommendations in our People's SWMP, and then we hope that this will allow us to work better with the council, Department of Sanitation, and all our stakeholders here to realize that vision of creating a more equitable plan. Thank you.

Thank you so much for your testimony. I do have a follow-up question. So one of the common threads of community conversation that has happened is wanting more specificity in the plan, wanting more attainable action items. From understanding— this is, you know, in 2006, I was a sophomore in high school. So from my understanding, I would like to understand better why advocates would like more– of course, you want things to hold people accountable for, but I think one of

the strengths also that you can argue with having such an open-ended language in the SWMP is we see how climate change is affecting us. We see how rapidly technology is evolving. We see all of these different things. Do we want— and we saw from the 2006— no, the 1992 SWMP, a lot of the projects and ideas that were talked about there that had actionable timelines, we don't even have the Fresh Kills landfill anymore. So my— I just wanna be understanding if we lock in some of these terms with what we see the world as we have it today, as opposed to having this open-end language so that folks can make adjustments. What do you see are the pros and cons? Is that a wrong way at looking at this, or is there a way to shift the mindset so that we can get both? Or how do you see that playing out?

Yeah. Thank you so much for your question. I think it's a mix of both because if the plan is too open-ended, like this is supposed to be essentially the floor for a lot of the policies that we will develop in the solid waste industry. So if it's too open-ended, then it doesn't really put a lot of consideration into a lot of the concerns that have been raised by community members. So I think

it's necessary for us to have like some more specificity around how some of the goals will be attained or how some of the benchmarks will be reached. Otherwise, like I said, it's just very open-ended. And you're right that things are constantly changing. So I think the plan does need to have some flexibility there, but on some of the more specific things, especially things that were brought up in the 2006 plan, which was a 20-year plan that haven't been done, like, what is the plan to actually get those done? I think those things need to be more specific while leaving the space to have that open-endedness that you mentioned. But right now it feels like it's just very open-ended and it's more of a framework as opposed to having like some of that specificity that's really needed for some of those areas.

Thank you. And one final follow-up question in terms of accountability. You mentioned stuff that hasn't been completed from previous SWMPs. Are there any accountability mechanisms that folks would like to see implemented that have not been used before or that you think are already working in terms of holding the department

accountable to, you know, frameworks and things that they put out?

Yeah. I mean, I don't think— I can't speak for like everyone who's here, everyone who's in the industry. But I think a lot of it— there are a lot of different– different mechanisms are needed for different areas. So I think like commercial waste zones was a thing that has been discussed a lot in this hearing and around commercial waste. And there were things that were mentioned around like having more GPS data and having things that DSNY is able to look at for a lot of the haulers. So I think just sort of looking at those avenues and ways in which that we are able to use this plan in order to create those accountability mechanisms. I think there was some suggestions mentioned earlier about, like maybe looking at NYCHA residents and how we could involve them more in the process. So I think it's— there's, like, definitely accountability around data as well. Like a lot of data is not very easily accessible or— and so if you're not getting the data that's easily accessible or easily understood, then you can't really hold the department accountable because you're not really sure

how accurate things are or what's happening. So I think there could definitely be like some more accountability around data, which I know is mentioned for Open Data, and then some more aspects for involving more community input in a lot of the processes and plans that are being developed, and then yeah, I know we talked about the commercial waste zone program as well and having some different avenues there, too.

And this just came to me, because we're talking about accountability, but not only department accountability, but are there ways that we can also be looking at personal accountability and ways that, you know, if folks are living in public housing or subsidized housing or vouchers and you are a repeat offender, non-recycler, or non-whatever that are really harming our communities, is there any accountability there? Is there— what does that look like, if that looks like anything at all? Has there been any conversation about that?

Yeah, I know. I personally haven't had conversations like that. I'm sure other folks here have had conversations around,

like, repeat offenders. I think like you mentioned earlier, like a lot of it does have to do with, I think, a cultural shift and understanding. I think there's like that cultural shift and understanding of the importance of our environment and what it means for us to do proper waste disposal and diversion and all the different things, and also just reduction, like waste. In this– we have a lot of waste that we're very wasteful. But I think also we have to make sure that the education is being carried out properly. I think we've heard from different avenues that education isn't really being done, and so sometimes you have repeat offenders because people don't know that they're supposed to be doing something or the way in which it's supposed to be done. So I think that having improved public education efforts is definitely necessary. I know that fines, everyone always thinks about money and how things are very expensive, so no one wants to get a fine. But I think first it has to be making sure that people actually understand what's required of them and what they need to be doing before we talk about fines and other mechanisms as well.
The problems of American consumerism.
[inaudible] American.
Thank you so much for your testimony. Hi, Justin.

Good afternoon. Thank you so much, Chair Sanchez, for holding this hearing and this opportunity, and congratulations to Commissioner Anderson, and thank you for the extensive testimony on topics including organics diversion, commercial waste zone implementation, and construction and demolition waste. We're looking forward— I'm sorry, I'm Justin Wood, New York Lawyers for the Public Interest, member of Transform Don't Trash. We're looking forward to working closely with the Council Sanitation Department and other parts of the Mamdani administration to implement all of this. We similarly have not fully read and compared the draft, and we do appreciate its publication on Friday, the revised draft SWMP. So we'll submit written comments. I can uplift a few themes from our previous comments from the 2025 SWMP hearing on this topic. On modeling, our understanding, unless this has changed, is that DSNY modeled increased diversion over 10 years. And we

understand that modeling needs to be grounded in the reality of New York City. We would also urge that the SWMP, because this is a long-term plan that we want to hold this administration and future administrations to, that modeling also include what it would take, what diversion rates would be necessary, or reduction rates in waste would be necessary to achieve the zero waste goals that the council and previous administration legislated, the community leadership, Climate Leadership and Community Protection Act emissions reduction goals that the state had set. We would stress that, you know, according to the state's estimates, solid waste produces almost as much greenhouse gas emissions as the entire electricity sector. So this is significant, and we want the state to also— because this is a DEC process— to see this as a pathway to implementing that law. So we would like to see some ambitious modeling included in the SWMP. I would just also highlight we'd like to see a plan for specific capital investments. We include– appreciate the reference to Rikers Island as a possible composting facility site. We'd like to see composting investments keep pace with the exciting developments

in the commercial and residential side with organics waste development. And then finally, we also will uplift the need to maximize the use of existing extensive capital investments in the marine and rail transfer facilities to study and, if necessary, subsidize the reduction of VMT fuel and operating costs, from simply taking some portion of commercial waste from places like Midtown Manhattan to a well-run, worker-friendly marine transfer station and avoiding trips to EJ communities. And then finally, we appreciate the stress on EPR as this extended producer responsibility is a potential source of long-term funding for these initiatives. We would similarly stress that the state, if it moves forward with a cap and invest program as called for in the current CLCPA, that that could be used as a major revenue source to help New York City implement these capital investments and programs. In the interim, we have called for the governor to implement a $3 billion Sustainable Futures Fund, and that's also— we'd like to see solid waste capital and program development as a major thing that those programs support. Thank you so much.
Thank you so much for your testimony.

Thank you, Chair Sanchez. Eric Goldstein of the Natural Resources Defense Council. The solid waste management planning process is a once-in-a-generation opportunity to rethink policy. We've got a new council, a new administration. We have a new commissioner, Greg Anderson, who's a good man, and we're happy he's on the scene. All of this– all of these issues affect the public in many ways, public health, quality of life, or economy. There's no rush. The council has legal authority to be involved in this planning process in a big way. According to 16-140 of the administrative code, no final solid waste management plan for the city shall be submitted to the state unless such submission has been authorized by the council by local law. So you already have the legal authority to be engaged in this process, and we hope the department will give the council the opportunity to review the revised draft and offer amendments to the plan before its final submission. This role of council oversight and engagement is essential, and the council should be full partners in the

development of this plan. In other words, the council should develop a set of amendments it believes should be included in the final SWMP. My written testimony, I outlined seven program areas where the plan, as strong as it is, should be strengthened. Let me just focus for a minute on organics. The organic section in particular needs some help. Organics is the largest portion of the waste stream. It's costing us a significant amount of money. Seattle has demonstrated that by composting organics, they are saving as much as $18 a ton according to their most recent data over landfilling it. So over time, as the IBO indicates, composting is not only beneficial for the environment but can save the city money. Right now the place to start is with food rescue where the verbiage is good, but much more can be done to ensure that all of the food generated in restaurants and commercial kitchens is sent over to help the 1.2 million New Yorkers who are food insecure. That's the place to start. And we need stronger elements on that. Then there's the issue of anaerobic co-digestion. That's the wrong way to deal with the organics that are collected. They should be actually composted. That means more composting capacity at

Rikers Island and other places. We need stronger marketing enforcement and educational materials in the schools, but also in the public more generally. We need to ensure that community composting is supported. We need legislation to advance commercial composting so that there's no question, but that every commercial establishment is separating its organics for composting. We set forth all of these recommendations in our written test testimony. Hope you will review them. Just one final word. The environmental justice issue, another area in need of strengthening. So you had talked before about job development and workforce development in NYCHA properties. Well, there's a program that has begun doing that. Compost Power is a nonprofit organization.
